title: Your Daily Checklist For Effective Classroom Management management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teaching, more than most professions, requires deliberate mental preparation before the school day begins, and he offers a short checklist meant to be reviewed every morning to put teachers in a consistent, effective state of mind. The checklist covers smiling and enjoying students, staying calm no matter the provocation, taking time rather than rushing, being specific about expectations, enforcing every classroom rule, and responding rather than reacting emotionally to misbehavior. He draws on a John Wooden maxim — 'Be quick but never in a hurry' — to illustrate the pace teachers should aim for in lessons and transitions. The article closes by encouraging teachers to print the checklist and run through it each morning, promising a noticeable difference in both student behavior and the teacher's own enjoyment of the day.
points: A brief morning ritual of mental preparation guards against the reactive mistakes that fuel misbehavior.
Staying calm and unhurried — 'quick but never in a hurry' — keeps students calmer and more focused.
Being specific about expectations, then stepping back, avoids micromanagement while still holding a clear standard.
Consistently enforcing every rule violation, regardless of the student, is central to an effective plan.
Choosing to respond rather than react (no yelling, scolding, or sarcasm) preserves trust and leverage with students.
quotes: If you’re feeling hurried, stressed, or distracted in the moments before the students arrive, teaching can be unforgiving—particularly in the area of classroom management.
A troop of kangaroos could bounce through your classroom, but you will remain the picture of poise.
The great basketball coach and teacher John Wooden was fond of saying, “Be quick but never in a hurry.” Keep your lessons and transitions sharp and moving, but with an efficient, deliberate pace.
By strictly enforcing your rules, you’re merely requiring behavior from your students that is necessary for success in school.

Decide that yelling, scolding, lecturing, arguing, and sarcasm won't be part of your classroom management repertoire. These reactions cause students to distrust and dislike you and lead to more misbehavior and less leverage.

I encourage you to print out this checklist and run through it each morning before your students arrive. I’m certain you’ll see a difference in your students’s behavior as well as your enjoyment of each day.
